position: both — *an insulting remark*; *that offer is insulting*
contrast: *insulting* describes the thing that offends; *insulted* describes the person who feels it: *his insulting tone left me insulted*.

senses.gloss: Rude enough to offend the person it is aimed at.
examples: His comment about my accent was *insulting*.
They made us an *insulting* offer for the car.
Nothing is more *insulting* than being talked down to.

position: both — *an insured driver*; *is your car insured?*
contrast: *The insured must file a claim within 30 days* uses a noun — the person who holds the policy.

senses.gloss: Covered by an insurance policy.
examples: Make sure the package is *insured* for the full value.
Only *insured* drivers can rent from this company.
The house is *insured* against flood damage.

position: both — *an insurmountable obstacle*; *the debt seemed insurmountable*

senses.gloss: Too great or too difficult to be overcome.
examples: The debt looked *insurmountable* at first.
None of these problems is *insurmountable*.
She faced *insurmountable* odds and finished the race anyway.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *the seal was intact*; before a noun: *an intact ecosystem*

senses.gloss: Whole and undamaged, with nothing missing or broken.
examples: The package arrived with the seal *intact*.
Somehow the old barn came through the storm *intact*.
Only one *intact* skeleton was found at the site.

position: both — *an intangible quality*; *the benefits are intangible*

senses.gloss: Real but hard to define, describe or measure.
examples: This team has an *intangible* quality that makes it win close games.
There is something *intangible* about her stage presence.
The benefits are real, but they are *intangible*.

senses.gloss: Not physical; impossible to touch.
examples: Patents and trademarks are *intangible* assets.
Software is *intangible*, but it still costs money.

position: both — *an integral part*; *music is integral to the show*
contrast: In math *an integral* is a noun, and that word is often stressed *in-TEG-ruhl*; the everyday adjective is stressed on the first syllable.

senses.gloss: So necessary that the whole thing is incomplete without it.
examples: Trust is an *integral* part of any partnership.
Her research was *integral* to the project's success.
Storytelling is *integral* to how this family remembers things.

senses.gloss: Built into a machine or structure rather than added on.
examples: The dishwasher has an *integral* water softener.
The frame and the seat are a single *integral* piece.

position: both — *an integrated system*; *the software is fully integrated*

senses.gloss: Combined with other parts into one system that works as a whole.
examples: The company runs an *integrated* accounting system.
The clinic is *integrated* with the main hospital.
These tools are more *integrated* than the ones we had before.

senses.gloss: Open to people of all races, not kept separate.
examples: He grew up in the first *integrated* neighborhood in town.
The schools here have been *integrated* since 1965.

position: both — *intellectual work*; *her friends are very intellectual*
contrast: *An intellectual* is also a noun for a person who works with ideas: *a room full of intellectuals*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the mind and with serious thinking.
examples: The job is *intellectual* rather than physical.
*Intellectual* property law gets complicated fast.
Chess gives him the *intellectual* challenge he needs.

senses.gloss: Interested in ideas and in books rather than in ordinary entertainment.
examples: Her friends are all quite *intellectual*.
He is too *intellectual* to sit through a silly movie.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *the recording is barely intelligible*
contrast: A trap: *intelligible* means 'able to be understood'; *intelligent* means 'smart'. A dog can be intelligent but not intelligible.

senses.gloss: Clear enough to be understood.
examples: The recording is barely *intelligible*.
Try to make your notes *intelligible* to someone else.
His speech got more *intelligible* after a few weeks of therapy.

position: both — before a noun: *the intended route*; after a verb with *for*: *the class is intended for beginners*

senses.gloss: Planned or meant for a particular person, purpose or result.
examples: The letter never reached its *intended* recipient.
This guide is *intended* for first-time buyers.
The joke had the opposite of its *intended* effect.

position: both — *intense heat*; *the pain was intense*
contrast: *intense* means very strong; *intensive* means packed into a short time or small space. A summer course is *intensive*, not *intense*.

senses.gloss: Very strong, sharp or extreme.
examples: The heat in August is *intense*.
She felt *intense* pain in her knee.
The second half was even more *intense* than the first.

senses.gloss: Of a person: very serious and focused, and feeling things strongly.
examples: He is an *intense* guy — he never really relaxes.
She gave me an *intense* look and said nothing.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an intensive course*; after a verb: *the training was intensive*
contrast: See *intense*. *Intensive care* is a hospital unit; *intense care* would mean something else entirely.

senses.gloss: Packing a great deal of work, effort or resources into a short time or small area.
examples: She took an *intensive* Spanish course over the summer.
He spent a week in *intensive* care.
Farming here is more *intensive* than it was fifty years ago.

position: both — *an intentional foul*; *the mistake was intentional*

senses.gloss: Done on purpose.
examples: The odd spelling in the title is *intentional*.
He was called for an *intentional* foul.
I'm sure the slight wasn't *intentional*.

position: both — *an interactive map*; *the lesson is interactive*

senses.gloss: Letting the user act and get a response, instead of only watching or reading.
examples: The museum has an *interactive* exhibit for kids.
Her lectures are *interactive* — she asks questions the whole time.
The new map is much more *interactive* than the old PDF.

position: both — *interchangeable parts*; *the two lenses are interchangeable*

senses.gloss: Able to be used in place of each other without any real difference.
examples: The two batteries are *interchangeable*.
In American English *cheap* and *inexpensive* are nearly *interchangeable*.
This lens is *interchangeable* with the one on my older camera.

position: attributive only — *intercollegiate sports*
contrast: *intercollegiate* games are between schools; *intramural* games are inside one campus.

senses.gloss: Held between two or more colleges or universities.
examples: He played *intercollegiate* tennis for four years.
The school dropped its *intercollegiate* wrestling program.
*Intercollegiate* athletics bring in a lot of money.

position: both — *an interconnected system*; *the two problems are interconnected*

senses.gloss: Joined to each other, so that each part affects the others.
examples: The two problems are *interconnected*.
We live in an *interconnected* world.
The caves form an *interconnected* system of tunnels.

position: attributive only — *an intercontinental flight*

senses.gloss: Going or carried between two continents.
examples: They took an *intercontinental* flight to Johannesburg.
The treaty limits *intercontinental* ballistic missiles.
He made his money in *intercontinental* shipping.

position: both — *an interdependent network*; *the two economies are interdependent*

senses.gloss: Depending on each other, so that neither one can manage alone.
examples: The two economies are deeply *interdependent*.
A forest is an *interdependent* web of plants and animals.
Team members grow more *interdependent* as the project goes on.

position: attributive only — *an interdisciplinary team*

senses.gloss: Bringing together more than one field of study.
examples: She works on an *interdisciplinary* team of doctors and engineers.
The college offers an *interdisciplinary* major in environmental studies.
*Interdisciplinary* research is harder to get funded.

position: attributive only — *an interest-bearing account*
form: compound — noun *interest* + the *-ing* participle of *bear*, 'to produce'

senses.gloss: Paying interest to whoever holds it.
examples: Put the money in an *interest-bearing* account.
The company issued *interest-bearing* notes.
They offer several *interest-bearing* savings options.

position: attributive only — *an interfaith service*

senses.gloss: Involving people from different religions.
examples: They held an *interfaith* service after the shooting.
She sits on the city's *interfaith* council.
*Interfaith* marriages are common in this neighborhood.

position: attributive only — *intergalactic travel*

senses.gloss: Between galaxies, or belonging to space beyond our own galaxy.
examples: The movie makes *intergalactic* travel look easy.
*Intergalactic* space is almost completely empty.
He writes *intergalactic* adventure novels for teenagers.

position: attributive only — *the interim director*
contrast: *In the interim* is a noun phrase meaning 'in the meantime', not the adjective.

senses.gloss: Holding a post or standing as a result only until the permanent one is in place.
examples: She is the *interim* dean until they hire someone.
The committee published an *interim* report in June.
The two sides reached an *interim* agreement last week.

position: attributive only — *interior walls*; for 'inside' after a verb use *inside*
contrast: *The interior of the car* is a noun. The adjective only goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: On or belonging to the inside of a building, vehicle or country.
examples: We are repainting the *interior* walls this weekend.
She works as an *interior* designer.
The country's *interior* provinces get very little rain.

position: attributive only — *interlocking pieces*

senses.gloss: Fitting into each other, or linked so that each part holds the others in place.
examples: The patio is made of *interlocking* tiles.
The novel tells three *interlocking* stories.
A set of *interlocking* deals kept the two firms together.

position: both — *an intermediate class*; *her Spanish is intermediate*
contrast: The adjective ends in a light *-dee-it*; the rarer verb *intermediate* ends in *-dee-ayt*.

senses.gloss: At the middle level, between beginner and advanced.
examples: She is in the *intermediate* Spanish class.
This trail is rated *intermediate*.
He plays at an *intermediate* level.

senses.gloss: Coming between two points, stages or things.
examples: The chemical is an *intermediate* step in the process.
The bus makes two *intermediate* stops before the airport.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an interminable meeting*; *the wait was interminable*
contrast: It always complains: an *interminable* speech is one that feels far too long, not one that literally has no end.

senses.gloss: Going on so long that it feels as if it will never end.
examples: We sat through an *interminable* speech.
The wait at the DMV was *interminable*.
He told an *interminable* story about his car.

position: both — *intermittent rain*; *the signal is intermittent*

senses.gloss: Stopping and starting again at uneven intervals rather than going on steadily.
examples: We had *intermittent* rain all afternoon.
The cell signal is *intermittent* out here.
She has *intermittent* pain in her shoulder.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *internal injuries*; *the bleeding was internal*

senses.gloss: Inside the body, or inside a machine or structure.
examples: She suffered *internal* injuries in the crash.
The engine has an *internal* cooling system.
The bleeding turned out to be *internal*.

senses.gloss: Inside one organization or country, not shared with outsiders.
examples: There is an *internal* investigation going on.
That memo was meant for *internal* use only.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *international law*; *the airport is international*

senses.gloss: Involving, or existing between, two or more countries.
examples: She flew out of the *international* terminal.
The band has a large *international* following.
*International* law says very little about this.

position: attributive only — *internecine fighting*

senses.gloss: Fought between members of the same group, and costly to both sides.
examples: *Internecine* fighting split the party in two.
Years of *internecine* warfare emptied the region.
The company lost its lead to *internecine* squabbling.

position: attributive only — *interpersonal skills*

senses.gloss: Between people; having to do with how people deal with one another.
examples: The job calls for strong *interpersonal* skills.
They brought in a coach to handle *interpersonal* conflicts.
Her *interpersonal* style works well with clients.

position: attributive only — *an interplanetary mission*

senses.gloss: Between the planets of our solar system.
examples: NASA is planning another *interplanetary* mission.
*Interplanetary* dust shows up clearly in the data.
The probe made the first *interplanetary* flight.

position: attributive only — *an interpretive center*
contrast: *interpretative* is the longer variant of the same word; Americans usually write *interpretive*.

senses.gloss: Explaining what something means, or resting on one person's reading of it.
examples: The park has an *interpretive* center near the entrance.
She gave an *interpretive* dance performance.
That is an *interpretive* question, not a factual one.

position: attributive only — *an interracial couple*

senses.gloss: Between or involving people of different races.
examples: *Interracial* marriage was illegal in some states until 1967.
They run an *interracial* church on the south side.
The film is about an *interracial* friendship in the 1950s.

position: both — *three interrelated questions*; *the issues are interrelated*

senses.gloss: Connected to each other, so that a change in one shows up in the others.
examples: Poverty and poor health are closely *interrelated*.
The book takes up three *interrelated* questions.
These problems are more *interrelated* than they look.

position: attributive only — *interstate commerce*
contrast: *An interstate* is also a noun for the highway itself, and it moves the stress to the front: *IN-tur-stayt*.

senses.gloss: Between two or more states of the United States.
examples: Congress regulates *interstate* commerce.
It is an *interstate* highway, so the speed limit is higher.
He was charged with *interstate* transport of stolen goods.

position: attributive only — *interstellar space*

senses.gloss: Between the stars.
examples: *Interstellar* travel is still science fiction.
The probe entered *interstellar* space in 2012.
Astronomers study clouds of *interstellar* gas.

position: attributive only — *the intervening years*

senses.gloss: Coming between two events in time, or between two places.
examples: In the *intervening* years he had married and moved away.
Nothing much happened in the *intervening* weeks.
An *intervening* ridge hides the lake from the house.

position: both — *interwoven strands*; *their lives are interwoven*

senses.gloss: Woven together, or so tightly connected that the parts cannot be pulled apart.
examples: The two families' histories are *interwoven*.
The rug is made of *interwoven* strips of wool.
The story is *interwoven* with letters and diary entries.

position: attributive only — *an intestinal infection*

senses.gloss: Of or inside the intestines.
examples: He picked up an *intestinal* bug on the trip.
The drug treats *intestinal* inflammation.
*Intestinal* bacteria help you digest food.

position: both — *an intimate friend*; *the two of them were intimate*
contrast: The verb *intimate*, meaning 'to hint', is said *IN-tuh-mayt*. The adjective ends in a short, weak *-mit*.

senses.gloss: Very close and personal, the way old friends or family members are.
examples: They have been *intimate* friends since childhood.
He put his most *intimate* thoughts in those letters.

senses.gloss: Sexual.
examples: The two of them had been *intimate* for a year.
She refused to discuss *intimate* details in court.

senses.gloss: Small, quiet and comfortable, in a way that feels private.
examples: It is an *intimate* little restaurant on a side street.
They had an *intimate* wedding with twelve guests.

senses.gloss: Detailed and thorough, from long first-hand experience.
examples: He has an *intimate* knowledge of the city's back streets.
She brought an *intimate* understanding of the law to the job.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *I felt intimidated*; *an intimidated witness*
contrast: *intimidated* is how the person feels; *intimidating* is what causes it: *the intimidating crowd left me intimidated*.

senses.gloss: Feeling nervous or afraid of someone or something bigger, stronger or more expert.
examples: I was *intimidated* by the size of the crowd.
Don't be *intimidated* — just ask your question.
New students often feel *intimidated* the first week.

position: both — *an intimidating figure*; *the form is intimidating*

senses.gloss: Making people feel nervous, small or afraid.
examples: He is an *intimidating* figure in the courtroom.
The first page of the form is the most *intimidating* part.
Her new boss turned out to be less *intimidating* than she expected.

position: both — *intolerable conditions*; *the noise became intolerable*

senses.gloss: So bad or so painful that nobody should have to put up with it.
examples: The noise from upstairs became *intolerable*.
They worked in *intolerable* conditions for years.
By noon the heat was *intolerable*.

position: both — *an intolerant attitude*; *he is intolerant of criticism*

senses.gloss: Unwilling to accept people who think, believe or live differently.
examples: He grew up in a small, *intolerant* town.
She is *intolerant* of any criticism at all.

senses.gloss: Unable to eat or take something without getting sick.
examples: My daughter is lactose *intolerant*.
Some people are *intolerant* of gluten.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *the driver was intoxicated*; *an intoxicated passenger*
contrast: A formal and legal word. In everyday speech Americans say *drunk*; police reports and court papers say *intoxicated*.

senses.gloss: Drunk, or under the influence of a drug.
examples: He was arrested for driving while *intoxicated*.
The passenger was clearly *intoxicated*.

senses.gloss: So excited by something that you cannot think clearly.
examples: They were *intoxicated* by their early success.
She came home *intoxicated* with the whole idea.

position: both — *an intoxicating smell*; *fame can be intoxicating*

senses.gloss: Exciting enough to carry you away and cloud your judgment.
examples: Fame can be *intoxicating*.
There was an *intoxicating* smell of lilacs in the yard.
That first summer of freedom was *intoxicating*.

senses.gloss: Containing alcohol.
examples: The statute covers all *intoxicating* liquors.
The county banned the sale of *intoxicating* beverages.

position: both — *an intractable problem*; *the dispute proved intractable*

senses.gloss: Very hard to solve or deal with.
examples: Homelessness is an *intractable* problem in big cities.
The dispute proved *intractable*, and the talks collapsed.

senses.gloss: Stubborn and hard to control.
examples: The mule was *intractable* that morning.
He can be *intractable* once he has made up his mind.

position: attributive only — *intramural sports*
contrast: *intramural* teams play other teams from the same school; *intercollegiate* teams play other schools.

senses.gloss: Played between teams from inside the same school, not against other schools.
examples: He plays *intramural* basketball on Tuesday nights.
The gym runs an *intramural* soccer league.
*Intramural* sports are open to every student.

position: both — *an intransigent position*; *both sides remained intransigent*

senses.gloss: Refusing to move from your position or to compromise at all.
examples: Both sides remained *intransigent* after three days of talks.
He took an *intransigent* line on taxes.
The union grew more *intransigent* as the strike dragged on.

position: attributive only — *intravenous fluids*
form: intra- ('inside') + *venous*, 'of the veins'; usually shortened to *IV*

senses.gloss: Going into a vein.
examples: She was put on *intravenous* antibiotics.
The nurse started an *intravenous* line in his arm.
*Intravenous* drug use spreads infection.

position: attributive only — *an intrepid explorer*
contrast: Often used half-jokingly today: *our intrepid reporter went out in the rain*.

senses.gloss: Brave and willing to go where others would not.
examples: The book follows an *intrepid* young explorer up the Amazon.
Our *intrepid* reporter stood outside in the hurricane.
A few *intrepid* swimmers went in anyway.

position: both — *an intricate pattern*; *the plot is intricate*

senses.gloss: Made of many small parts or details arranged in a complicated way.
examples: The gate has an *intricate* iron design.
The plot is *intricate* but easy enough to follow.
Her later quilts are even more *intricate* than the early ones.

position: both — *an intriguing idea*; *the ending is intriguing*

senses.gloss: Interesting enough to make you want to know more.
examples: She made an *intriguing* suggestion at the meeting.
The most *intriguing* part is the last chapter.
There is something *intriguing* about that old house.

position: both — *intrinsic value*; *risk is intrinsic to the job*

senses.gloss: Belonging to something by its own nature, rather than added from outside.
examples: The coin's *intrinsic* value is far less than its price.
Some risk is *intrinsic* to any investment.
She talks about the *intrinsic* rewards of teaching.

position: attributive only — *an introductory course*

senses.gloss: Coming at the beginning, to explain what follows.
examples: Read the *introductory* chapter first.
She teaches an *introductory* statistics course.

senses.gloss: Offered at a low price to bring in new customers.
examples: The *introductory* rate lasts six months.
It is nine dollars at the *introductory* price.

position: both — *an introspective album*; *he grew introspective*

senses.gloss: Spending a lot of time examining your own thoughts and feelings.
examples: He is a quiet, *introspective* kid.
Her later albums are more *introspective* than the first two.
The long illness made him *introspective*.

position: both — *an introverted child*; *she is fairly introverted*
contrast: *introverted* is not the same as *shy*: an introvert may be perfectly confident and still prefer a quiet evening.

senses.gloss: Happier alone or in small groups than in a crowd, and quiet with strangers.
examples: She is *introverted* but not at all shy.
Our team is full of *introverted* engineers.
He has gotten more *introverted* since the move.

position: both — *an intrusive question*; *the ads are intrusive*

senses.gloss: Pushing into someone's private life or space in a way that is not welcome.
examples: The questions felt *intrusive*.
The ads on that site are more *intrusive* every year.
He apologized for being *intrusive*.

position: both — *an intuitive design*; *the controls are intuitive*

senses.gloss: Easy to understand and use without being taught.
examples: The new app is much more *intuitive*.
These controls are not very *intuitive* to a first-time user.

senses.gloss: Based on a feeling rather than on conscious reasoning.
examples: She made an *intuitive* decision and it paid off.
He is an *intuitive* player, not an analytical one.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *the office was inundated with calls*

senses.gloss: Given far more of something than you can possibly handle.
examples: We were *inundated* with applications.
The help desk is *inundated* every Monday morning.

senses.gloss: Covered by a flood of water.
examples: Whole neighborhoods were *inundated* by the storm surge.
The fields stayed *inundated* for weeks.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *inured to the cold*

senses.gloss: So used to something unpleasant that it no longer bothers you.
examples: Nurses become *inured* to the sight of blood.
He is *inured* to the cold after ten winters up there.
You never get fully *inured* to bad news.

position: both — *an invalid password*; *the contract is invalid*
contrast: The noun *invalid*, meaning a person weakened by illness, is a different word stressed on the first syllable: *IN-vuh-lid*.

senses.gloss: Not legally or officially acceptable.
examples: Your passport is *invalid* once it expires.
The court declared the contract *invalid*.

senses.gloss: Not resting on sound reasoning or good evidence.
examples: That is an *invalid* argument.
The study's conclusion turned out to be *invalid*.

position: both — *invaluable help*; *her advice was invaluable*
contrast: A real trap: *invaluable* does not mean 'not valuable'. It means 'too valuable to put a price on'. The opposite is *worthless*, not *valuable*.

senses.gloss: So useful or so valuable that no price could be put on it.
examples: Her advice was *invaluable*.
He is an *invaluable* member of the team.
Those old photographs are *invaluable* to the family.

position: both — *an invasive species*; *the test is invasive*

senses.gloss: Spreading fast into places where it does not belong, or into healthy tissue.
examples: Kudzu is an *invasive* species in the South.
The tumor turned out to be *invasive*.

senses.gloss: Of a medical procedure: involving cutting or putting instruments inside the body.
examples: They chose the least *invasive* surgery available.
It is a quick, non-*invasive* test.

senses.gloss: Pushing into private matters in an unwelcome way.
examples: The security screening felt *invasive*.
She asked a few *invasive* questions about my salary.

position: both — *an inventive solution*; *the chef is inventive*

senses.gloss: Good at thinking up new ideas or new ways of doing things.
examples: The chef here is remarkably *inventive*.
It is an *inventive* solution to a very old problem.
Her second novel is more *inventive* than the first.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an inverse relationship*; *the two effects are inverse to each other*
contrast: *The inverse* is also a noun in math, and there the stress moves forward: *IN-vurs*.

senses.gloss: Moving in the opposite direction, so that one goes up as the other goes down.
examples: There is an *inverse* relationship between price and demand.
Attendance fell in *inverse* proportion to ticket prices.
The two effects are *inverse* to each other.

position: both — *an inverted pyramid*; *the image is inverted*

senses.gloss: Turned upside down, or put into the opposite order.
examples: News stories use an *inverted* pyramid structure.
The image in the mirror is *inverted*.
He wore an *inverted* cross on a chain.

position: attributive only — *investigative journalism*

senses.gloss: Doing or involving careful digging into facts, especially where something has gone wrong.
examples: She won a prize for *investigative* journalism.
The *investigative* team spent a year on the story.
He heads the bureau's *investigative* division.

position: attributive only — *investigatory powers*
contrast: *investigative* is the everyday word; *investigatory* turns up mostly in legal writing about official powers and procedures.

senses.gloss: Having to do with an official investigation.
examples: The committee has broad *investigatory* powers.
The agency opened an *investigatory* file on the company.
Her lawyers challenged the board's *investigatory* process.

position: attributive only — *an inveterate gambler*
contrast: It goes with a person and a long-standing habit, usually a bad one: *an inveterate liar*. You cannot say *the habit is inveterate* about a person.

senses.gloss: Having done something for so long that it will never change.
examples: He is an *inveterate* gambler.
My uncle is an *inveterate* storyteller.
She is an *inveterate* collector of old maps.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an invidious comparison*; *it would be invidious to choose*

senses.gloss: Unfair in a way that is bound to offend someone or stir up bad feeling.
examples: It would be *invidious* to name only three of them.
He drew an *invidious* comparison between the two sisters.
The ranking puts her in an *invidious* position.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *I felt invigorated*

senses.gloss: Filled with fresh energy and strength.
examples: I always feel *invigorated* after a swim.
She came back from vacation *invigorated*.
The crowd left the team *invigorated* for the second half.

position: both — *an invigorating walk*; *the cold air was invigorating*

senses.gloss: Giving you fresh energy.
examples: The cold morning air was *invigorating*.
She took an *invigorating* walk before breakfast.
Nothing is more *invigorating* than a swim in the lake.

position: both — *an invincible army*; *the team looked invincible*

senses.gloss: Impossible to beat or defeat.
examples: At seventeen you feel *invincible*.
The team looked *invincible* all season.
No army is truly *invincible*.

position: both — *an inviolable rule*; *these rights are inviolable*

senses.gloss: That must never be broken, attacked or interfered with.
examples: They treat that rule as *inviolable*.
The constitution calls these rights *inviolable*.
Sunday dinner at Grandma's was an *inviolable* tradition.

position: both — *invisible ink*; *the crack is invisible*

senses.gloss: Impossible to see.
examples: *Invisible* ink shows up under a black light.
The crack is nearly *invisible* from the street.
Radio waves are *invisible* to us.

senses.gloss: Present but ignored, as if nobody could see you.
examples: She felt *invisible* at the party.
Night-shift workers are *invisible* to most of the company.

position: both — *an inviting room*; *the water looked inviting*

senses.gloss: Attractive enough to make you want to come in, sit down or try it.
examples: The kitchen smelled warm and *inviting*.
The lake looked *inviting* on a day like that.
Their new lobby is much more *inviting* than the old one.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an involuntary gasp*; *the layoffs were involuntary*

senses.gloss: Happening by itself, without your choosing it.
examples: Blinking is an *involuntary* movement.
She gave an *involuntary* gasp when the lights went out.

senses.gloss: Forced on someone who did not agree to it.
examples: He faces *involuntary* commitment to a hospital.
Most of the layoffs were *involuntary*.

position: both — *an invulnerable position*; *no system is invulnerable*

senses.gloss: Impossible to harm, attack or damage.
examples: No system is *invulnerable* to attack.
He acted as though he were *invulnerable*.
They built an *invulnerable* lead by halftime.

position: attributive only — *an inward journey*
contrast: *inward* is also an adverb — *the door swings inward* — and Americans also say *inwards* for the adverb. The adjective only goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: Turned toward the inside, or belonging to your private thoughts.
examples: The novel describes a long *inward* journey.
She gave an *inward* groan and kept smiling.
The latch needs a short *inward* push to release.

position: attributive only — *iodized salt*
form: from *iodine*, the element added to it

senses.gloss: Treated with iodine.
examples: Use *iodized* salt unless the recipe says otherwise.
*Iodized* salt prevents a common thyroid problem.
The store carries only *iodized* table salt.

position: both — *an Iranian film*; *her parents are Iranian*
contrast: *An Iranian* is also a noun for a person from Iran. *Persian* usually names the language and the older culture, not the modern country. Always capitalized.

senses.gloss: From Iran, or having to do with Iran.
examples: We ate at a new *Iranian* restaurant downtown.
She studies *Iranian* film at the university.
His parents are *Iranian*.

position: both — *the Iraqi government*; *her husband is Iraqi*
contrast: *An Iraqi* is also a noun for a person from Iraq. Always capitalized.

senses.gloss: From Iraq, or having to do with Iraq.
examples: He met an *Iraqi* family at the clinic.
The *Iraqi* government issued a statement this morning.
Her husband is *Iraqi*.

position: both — *an irascible old man*; *he gets irascible when he's tired*

senses.gloss: Quick to lose your temper over small things.
examples: The old man was famously *irascible*.
He gets more *irascible* every year.
She plays an *irascible* judge in the series.

position: both — *an irate customer*; *the neighbors were irate*

senses.gloss: Very angry.
examples: An *irate* customer demanded a refund.
The neighbors were *irate* about the noise.
She wrote an *irate* letter to the editor.

position: both — *an iridescent shell*; *the bubbles are iridescent*

senses.gloss: Showing shifting rainbow colors as the light or the angle changes.
examples: The beetle's shell is *iridescent*.
She wore an *iridescent* green dress.
Soap bubbles look *iridescent* in the sun.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an ironclad guarantee*; *his alibi was ironclad*
contrast: The literal sense, 'armored with iron', survives mostly in *an ironclad warship* and in the noun *an ironclad*.

senses.gloss: So firm that nothing can break it or get around it.
examples: We offer an *ironclad* guarantee on parts and labor.
His alibi was *ironclad*.
They signed an *ironclad* contract.

position: both — *an ironic smile*; *it's ironic that he lost*

senses.gloss: Saying the opposite of what you mean, to be funny or cutting.
examples: His tone was *ironic*, not sincere.
She made an *ironic* remark about the weather.

senses.gloss: Odd in a way that seems like a joke played by fate.
examples: It is *ironic* that the fire station burned down.
In an *ironic* twist, he ended up working for the company he sued.

position: both — *an irrational fear*; *he gets irrational when he's tired*

senses.gloss: Not based on reason or clear thinking.
examples: She has an *irrational* fear of bridges.
He gets *irrational* when he hasn't slept.
The more he drank, the more *irrational* he became.

position: both — *irreconcilable differences*; *the two accounts are irreconcilable*

senses.gloss: So different that they can never be brought into agreement.
examples: They divorced over *irreconcilable* differences.
The two versions of the story are *irreconcilable*.
His account is *irreconcilable* with the video.

position: both — *an irredeemable mess*; *nobody is irredeemable*

senses.gloss: Too bad to be fixed, saved or forgiven.
examples: The script isn't *irredeemable* — it just needs work.
He wrote the whole season off as *irredeemable*.
She doesn't believe anyone is *irredeemable*.

position: both — *irrefutable evidence*; *the logic is irrefutable*
contrast: Also commonly said *ih-REF-yuh-tuh-buhl*, with the stress pulled back to the second syllable.

senses.gloss: Impossible to argue against or disprove.
examples: The DNA evidence was *irrefutable*.
He made an *irrefutable* case for the change.
The logic here is *irrefutable*.

position: both — *an irregular heartbeat*; *the shape is irregular*

senses.gloss: Not happening at even intervals.
examples: He keeps *irregular* hours.
Her heartbeat was *irregular*, so they kept her overnight.

senses.gloss: Not even or smooth in shape or surface.
examples: The patio is laid with stones of *irregular* shapes.
The coastline here is wild and *irregular*.

senses.gloss: Not following the usual rule or the proper procedure.
examples: *Go* is an *irregular* verb.
The hiring process was highly *irregular*.

position: both — *an irrelevant question*; *his age is irrelevant*

senses.gloss: Having nothing to do with the matter being discussed.
examples: That fact is *irrelevant* to the case.
The judge ruled the question *irrelevant*.
His age is completely *irrelevant* here.

position: attributive only — *irreparable damage*; after a verb say *beyond repair*
contrast: The stress falls on *-REP-*, not on *-PAIR-*: *ih-REP-ur-uh-buhl*, even though it comes from *repair*.

senses.gloss: Too badly damaged to be repaired or put right.
examples: The flood did *irreparable* damage to the archive.
His reputation suffered *irreparable* harm.
The argument caused an *irreparable* break between the brothers.

position: both — *an irreplaceable coach*; *those photos are irreplaceable*

senses.gloss: So rare or so special that nothing else could take its place.
examples: Those family photographs are *irreplaceable*.
She is an *irreplaceable* part of this office.
The fire destroyed *irreplaceable* records.

position: both — *an irrepressible optimist*; *the puppy is irrepressible*

senses.gloss: So full of energy or good spirits that nothing can hold it back.
examples: Her *irrepressible* laugh carried across the room.
He is an *irrepressible* optimist.
The puppy is *irrepressible* before breakfast.
